questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes the direction of conventional electric current?

options.text: From the negative terminal to the positive terminal of a cell
The same as the direction of the electrons' flow
The direction is random and charges flow in a constant way
From the positive terminal to the negative terminal of a cell

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**From the positive terminal to the negative terminal of a cell**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 

__ 
 
• **Conventional current** flows from the **positive terminal to the negative terminal of a cell**. This direction was historically defined before the discovery of electrons. 
 
• The **electrons' flow**, or the actual flow of charge carriers in most metallic conductors, is in the **opposite direction** of the conventional current. 
 
• The direction of conventional current is based on the assumption that **positive charges move**, even though in most cases (like in metals), negative electrons are the actual charge carriers. 
 
• The statement "From the negative terminal to the positive terminal of a cell" is incorrect because it describes the **electron flow**, not the conventional current. 
 
• The conventional direction of current is used in circuit diagrams and analysis, regardless of the type of charge carriers in the material. *Hence, the correct answer is "From the positive terminal to the negative terminal of a cell."* 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 

__ 
 
• **Electron Flow vs Conventional Current:** 
 
 
• Electrons flow from the **negative terminal** to the **positive terminal** of a cell because they are negatively charged and are attracted to the positive terminal. 
 
• Conventional current assumes that positive charges flow from the **positive terminal** to the **negative terminal**. This convention was established before the discovery of the electron. 
 
 
 
• **Electric Current:** 
 
 
• Electric current is defined as the **rate of flow of electric charge**. In metals, this charge is carried by electrons. 
 
• The unit of current is the **ampere (A)**, and it is measured using an **ammeter**. 
 
 
 
• **Real-world Applications:** 
 
 
• In electronic circuits, the conventional current direction is used for designing and analyzing circuits, regardless of the type of charge carriers (positive ions, electrons, etc.). 
 
• In electrolytes, both **positive and negative ions** contribute to the current, but the conventional current direction is still from positive to negative. 
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:** 
 
 
• The concept of conventional current was introduced by **Benjamin Franklin** in the 18th century, long before the discovery of the electron in 1897 by **J.J. Thomson**. 
 
• Franklin assumed that the charge carriers were positive, leading to the convention of current flowing from positive to negative. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 

 
 
• **Direction of Current in Different Materials:** 
 
 
• In metallic conductors, current is due to the movement of **free electrons**. 
 
• In semiconductors, both **electrons** and **holes** contribute to current flow. 
 
• In electrolytic solutions, current is carried by the movement of **positive and negative ions**. 
 
 
 
• **Practical Relevance:** 
 
 
• Although the electron flow is opposite to the conventional current, the latter is universally used in circuit analysis for simplicity and consistency.

questions.question: In which part of the neurons, is the first electrical impulse created?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dendrite**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__
 
__ 

• **Dendrites** are the branch-like extensions of a neuron that receive signals from other neurons or external stimuli. The first electrical impulse is generated here when the dendrites detect a stimulus. 

• These impulses are the result of the movement of ions across the neuronal membrane, which creates an electrical signal known as an **action potential**. 

• The dendrites play a crucial role in the **initial phase of signal transmission**, where they collect and process incoming signals before relaying them to the cell body. 

• The electrical signals collected by the dendrites are transmitted to the **axon hillock**, where the decision to generate a full-fledged action potential is made. 

• The dendritic structure ensures that neurons can process multiple incoming signals simultaneously, enabling complex neurological functions. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
 

• **Structure of a Neuron:** 
 

• A neuron consists of three main parts: **dendrites**, a **cell body**, and an **axon**. 

• The **dendrites** receive signals, the **cell body** processes them, and the **axon** transmits the signals to the next neuron or target tissue. 
 
 

• **Role of Dendrites in Signal Transmission:** 
 

• Dendrites primarily function as **receivers of chemical or electrical signals** from other neurons or sensory organs. 

• The signals received are converted into small electrical changes called **graded potentials**, which travel toward the cell body. 
 
 

• **Action Potential:** 
 

• The electrical impulse in a neuron is called an **action potential**, a rapid change in electrical charge across the membrane that allows signals to travel along the neuron. 

• Action potentials are initiated only if the signals received by the dendrites and cell body reach a certain threshold at the **axon hillock**. 
 
 

• **Functions of Neuronal Components:** 
 

• **Cell Body (Soma):** Contains the nucleus and organelles; integrates incoming signals. 

• **Axon:** Conducts electrical impulses away from the cell body to other neurons or muscles. 

• **Nerve Endings:** Release neurotransmitters to communicate with other cells. 
 
 

• **Examples of Neuron Types:** 
 

• **Motor Neurons:** Carry signals from the central nervous system to muscles. 

• **Sensory Neurons:** Transmit sensory information like touch, heat, and pain to the brain. 

• **Interneurons:** Facilitate communication between sensory and motor neurons. 
 
 
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding cells?

options.text: Cells can be round, oval, spindle-shaped or branched.
All cells are of the same size and shape.
Nerve cells are long to help in the conduction of impulses.
Cell shape is often related to its function.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**All cells are of the same size and shape.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Cells can be round, oval, spindle-shaped, or branched:** The shape of cells varies significantly depending on their type and function. For instance, red blood cells are biconcave, while nerve cells are elongated. *This statement is correct.*
 
• **All cells are of the same size and shape:** This is a false statement. Cells vary greatly in size and shape based on their role in the body. For example, a human egg cell is much larger than a red blood cell, and nerve cells are elongated to transmit signals efficiently. *This statement is incorrect.*
 
• **Nerve cells are long to help in the conduction of impulses:** Nerve cells (neurons) have long extensions called axons that are adapted for transmitting electrical impulses over long distances. This structural adaptation supports their function. *This statement is correct.*
 
• **Cell shape is often related to its function:** The shape of a cell is closely linked to its function. For example, muscle cells are elongated to facilitate contraction, and epithelial cells are flat to form protective layers. *This statement is correct.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Variation in cell size:**
 
 
• The size of cells varies greatly. For example, bacterial cells are typically 1-10 micrometers in size, while human egg cells can reach up to 100 micrometers.
 
• Some specialized cells, like neurons, can extend over a meter in length in large organisms.
 
 
 
• **Variation in cell shape:**
 
 
• Cell shapes are highly diverse and adapted to their functions. For instance:
 
 
• Red blood cells are disc-shaped to maximize surface area for oxygen exchange.
 
• Guard cells in plants are kidney-shaped to facilitate opening and closing of stomata.
 
• Nerve cells have branching structures for communication with other cells.
 
 
 
 
 
• **Structure and function correlation:**
 
 
• The relationship between structure and function is a fundamental principle in biology. For example:
 
 
• Muscle cells contain actin and myosin proteins for contraction.
 
• Leaf cells have chloroplasts to perform photosynthesis.
 
 
 
 
 
• **Cell diversity in organisms:**
 
 
• Multicellular organisms have specialized cells for different functions, such as blood cells for oxygen transport, immune cells for defense, and skin cells for protection.
 
• Unicellular organisms like amoebas perform all life processes within a single cell.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Examples of cell specialization:**
 
 
• Red blood cells lack nuclei to maximize space for hemoglobin, which transports oxygen.
 
• Root hair cells in plants have long extensions to increase surface area for water absorption.
 
 
 
• **Discovery of cells:**
 
 
• Cells were first discovered by **Robert Hooke** in **1665** when he observed cork under a microscope.
 
• The cell theory, proposed by **Schleiden** and **Schwann**, states that all living organisms are composed of cells, which are the basic unit of life.
 
 
 
• **Cell types:**
 
 
• Prokaryotic cells lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles (e.g., bacteria).
 
• Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and specialized organelles (e.g., animal and plant cells).
 
 
</ul

questions.question: The blades of a windmill rotate because of which of the following?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Wind’s kinetic energy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The blades of a windmill rotate due to the **kinetic energy of the wind**. When the wind blows, it transfers its kinetic energy to the blades, causing them to move.
 
• As the wind strikes the blades, it exerts a force on them. The design of the blades, often curved or tilted, ensures that this force causes rotation.
 
• The rotation of the windmill blades is then converted into other forms of energy, typically **mechanical energy**, which is used for tasks such as pumping water or grinding grains.
 
• In modern wind turbines, the mechanical energy is further converted into **electrical energy** via a generator, contributing to sustainable energy production.
 
• This process exemplifies the principle of energy conversion, where the wind's kinetic energy is transformed into usable forms of energy, reducing dependency on fossil fuels.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Kinetic Energy:**

 
 
• Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by an object due to its motion.
 
• The formula for kinetic energy is given by **KE = 1/2 mv²**, where **m** is the mass of the object and **v** is its velocity.
 
• In the case of wind, the moving air molecules possess kinetic energy that can be harnessed for various purposes.
 
 
 
• **Wind Energy:**
 
 
• Wind energy is a form of **renewable energy** derived from the movement of air in the Earth's atmosphere.
 
• It is a clean and sustainable source of energy, widely used in generating electricity through wind turbines.
 
• Countries like **China, the United States, and Germany** are global leaders in wind energy production.
 
• Wind energy contributes significantly to reducing greenhouse gas emissions and combating climate change.
 
 
 
• **Windmill Design:**
 
 
• Windmill blades are designed aerodynamically to optimize the capture of wind energy.
 
• The shape and angle of the blades ensure that they catch maximum wind, creating a lift force that causes rotation.
 
• Modern wind turbines can adjust the angle of their blades (pitch control) to regulate energy production based on wind speed.
 
 
 
• **Other Forms of Energy:**
 
 
• While the question mentions other forms of energy like light, elastic, and sound energy, they are not responsible for the rotation of windmill blades.
 
• **Light energy** is typically associated with solar power, while **elastic energy** relates to materials under tension or compression.
 
• **Sound energy** refers to the energy carried by sound waves and does not have the capacity to rotate windmill blades.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Global Wind Energy Statistics:**

 
 
• As of **2022**, global wind power capacity exceeded **800 GW**, according to the Global Wind Energy Council.
 
• India ranks among the top countries for wind energy production, with states like **Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, and Maharashtra** leading in installations.
 
 
 
• **Advantages of Wind Energy:**
 
 
• It is a **renewable** and **eco-friendly** source of energy.
 
• Wind turbines have a low operational cost once installed.
 
• They reduce reliance on fossil fuels and help in achieving energy security.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in Wind Energy:**
 
 
• Wind energy production is location-dependent, requiring areas with consistent wind speeds.
 
• High initial investment costs can be a barrier to widespread adoption.
 
• The intermittent nature of wind can pose challenges to grid stability without energy storage systems.

questions.question: A force of 50 N acts perpendicular to a surface of area 0.1 { m}² . What are the values of thrust and pressure exerted on the surface?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Thrust = 50.0 N; Pressure = 500.0 Pa**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 

• **Thrust:** Thrust is the force acting perpendicular to a surface. In this case, a force of **50 N** acts perpendicular to the surface. This means the thrust is **50 N**. Hence, the value of thrust is correct. 

• **Pressure:** Pressure is defined as force per unit area. The formula is: 
 
 
• Pressure = Force ÷ Area 
 
• Given force = **50 N**, Area = **0.1 m²** 
 
• Pressure = 50 ÷ 0.1 = **500 Pa** 
 
 

• The provided values for thrust (**50 N**) and pressure (**500 Pa**) are consistent with the given conditions and calculations. 

• Thus, the correct option is **Thrust = 50.0 N; Pressure = 500.0 Pa**. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **Thrust:** 
 
 
• Thrust is a vector quantity that acts perpendicular to the surface it is applied to. 
 
• In this problem, thrust is equal to the given force, as the force is applied perpendicular to the surface. 
 
• Unit: The SI unit of thrust is the **Newton (N)**. 
 
• Applications: Thrust plays a crucial role in various fields, such as fluid dynamics, aerodynamics, and engineering. 
 
 

• **Pressure:** 
 
 
• Pressure is a scalar quantity and is defined as force applied per unit area. 
 
• Formula: Pressure = Force ÷ Area 
 
• Unit: The SI unit of pressure is the **Pascals (Pa)**. 1 Pa = 1 N/m². 
 
• Applications: Pressure is widely used in fluid mechanics, hydraulics, and meteorology. 
 
• Examples: Atmospheric pressure, blood pressure, and pressure in hydraulic systems. 
 
 

• **Relationship between force, area, and pressure:** 
 
 
• As the area decreases for a given force, the pressure increases. 
 
• Conversely, as the area increases for a given force, the pressure decreases. 
 
 

• **Units and Conversion:** 
 
 
• Pressure in Pascals can be converted into other units like bar, atmosphere, and mmHg (millimeter of mercury). 
 
• 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa, 1 atm = 101325 Pa, and 1 mmHg = 133.322 Pa. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 

• **Factors affecting pressure:** 
 
 
• Force: Higher force leads to greater pressure if the area remains constant. 
 
• Area: Smaller area leads to greater pressure if the force remains constant. 
 
 

• **Real-life applications of pressure:** 
 
 
• In tire design: Pressure is critical for maintaining proper traction and safety. 
 
• In hydraulics: Hydraulic systems use pressure to lift heavy objects. 
 
• In weather prediction: Atmospheric pressure variations help predict weather conditions. 
 
 

• **Thrust in fluid mechanics:** 
 
 
• Thrust is used in propulsion systems of rockets, planes, and submarines. 
 
• It is also used to measure aerodynamic forces in wind tunnels.

questions.question: What is the atomic number of an element that has 17 electrons and 18 neutrons?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**17**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 
 
• **Atomic Number:** The atomic number of an element is determined by the number of **protons** in its nucleus. Since the number of protons equals the number of electrons in a neutral atom, an element with **17 electrons** has an atomic number of **17**. *This is correct.* 
 
• **Chlorine:** The element with an atomic number of 17 is **chlorine (Cl)**. It is a halogen and is known for its high reactivity. 
 
• **Neutrons:** The number of neutrons in an atom can be calculated using the formula: **Mass Number = Protons + Neutrons**. If the atom has 17 protons and 18 neutrons, its mass number is **35**. This matches the most common isotope of chlorine, **chlorine-35**. *This is correct.* 
 
• **Electron Configuration:** Chlorine’s electron configuration is **2, 8, 7**, indicating it belongs to Group 17 of the periodic table (halogens). 
 
• **Periodic Table Position:** With an atomic number of 17, chlorine is positioned in the **third period** and the **p-block** of the periodic table. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
 
 
• **Chlorine in Nature:** Chlorine is commonly found in compounds such as **sodium chloride (table salt)**. It is abundant in seawater and is also found in minerals such as halite. 
 
• **Uses of Chlorine:** Chlorine is widely used in **water purification**, **bleaching agents**, and in the production of **plastics** like PVC (polyvinyl chloride). 
 
• **Isotopes:** Chlorine has two stable isotopes: **chlorine-35** (about 76% abundance) and **chlorine-37** (about 24% abundance). The average atomic mass of chlorine is approximately **35.5 u** due to these isotopes. 
 
• **Halogen Properties:** As a halogen, chlorine is highly reactive and forms compounds readily. It often forms **ionic bonds** with metals and **covalent bonds** with nonmetals. 
 
• **Safety Considerations:** Chlorine gas is highly toxic and was historically used as a chemical weapon. Proper safety measures are essential when handling chlorine.

questions.question: Which of the following best demonstrates that there is a space between particles of matter?

options.text: A piece of chalk breaks easily

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sugar dissolves in water**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 
 
• **Sugar dissolving in water** demonstrates that there are spaces between particles of matter. When sugar is added to water, it breaks down into smaller particles that occupy the spaces between the water molecules. 
 
• This phenomenon is possible because **particles of matter are not tightly packed** and have spaces between them, allowing other particles to fit in. 
 
• During dissolution, the sugar particles interact with water molecules through **intermolecular forces**, dispersing evenly in the liquid. 
 
• The process of sugar dissolving also illustrates the concept of **solubility**, which is determined by the nature of both the solute (sugar) and solvent (water). 
 
• It serves as evidence for the **kinetic theory of matter**, which states that particles are in constant motion and have spaces between them. ***Hence, this option is correct.*** 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 
 
• **Intermolecular Space:** 
 
• All matter is made of particles, and these particles have **spaces between them**. 
 
• The magnitude of these spaces varies depending on the **state of matter** (solid, liquid, or gas). 
 
• **Solids:** Particles are tightly packed with minimal intermolecular space. 
 
• **Liquids:** Particles have moderate space, allowing them to flow. 
 
• **Gases:** Particles have maximum space and move freely. 
 
 
• **Solubility:** 
 
• Solubility is the ability of a substance to dissolve in a solvent, forming a solution. 
 
• Sugar dissolves in water due to its **polar nature**, which matches the polarity of water. 
 
• Temperature and pressure are factors that can affect the solubility of substances. 
 
 
• **Kinetic Theory of Matter:** 
 
• According to this theory, particles are in constant motion, and their movement depends on the **state of matter**. 
 
• In liquids, the movement of particles allows substances like sugar to dissolve by filling the spaces between water molecules. 
 
 
• **Other Observations:** 
 
• **A rubber band stretches:** It demonstrates elasticity, not spaces between particles. 
 
• **Ice melts into water:** This indicates a change of state due to heat, not the concept of spaces between particles. 
 
• **A piece of chalk breaks easily:** It illustrates brittleness, which is unrelated to intermolecular spaces. 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 
 
• **Experimental Evidence:** The dissolution of sugar in water can be observed during practical experiments, providing a clear understanding of intermolecular spaces. 
 
• **Applications:** The concept of spaces between particles is crucial in understanding various phenomena, such as diffusion, solubility, and state changes. 
 
• **Daily Life Examples:** Dissolving salt, mixing drinks, and diffusion of perfume are instances where intermolecular spaces play a significant role. 
 
• **Scientific Basis:** Studies on molecular structure, forces, and behavior have provided detailed insights into the nature of matter and particle interaction. 
</ul

questions.question: Which among the following covalent compounds will have the least number of shared electron pairs?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**H₂**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 

__ 
 
• **Covalent compounds** are formed when atoms share electrons to achieve a full outer shell and attain stability. Each shared pair of electrons forms a covalent bond. 
 
• **O₂** (Oxygen molecule): Consists of a double bond between two oxygen atoms, which means it involves two shared pairs of electrons (4 electrons in total). 
 
• **N₂** (Nitrogen molecule): Consists of a triple bond between two nitrogen atoms, meaning it involves three shared pairs of electrons (6 electrons in total). 
 
• **CH₄** (Methane): Each hydrogen atom shares one electron with the carbon atom, forming four single covalent bonds. Therefore, methane has 4 shared electron pairs. 
 
• **H₂** (Hydrogen molecule): Consists of a single covalent bond between two hydrogen atoms, involving only one shared pair of electrons (2 electrons in total). This is the **least number of shared electron pairs**. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 

__ 
 
• **Covalent Bonding:** 
 
 
• Occurs between non-metallic elements where atoms share electrons to achieve a stable electronic configuration (similar to a noble gas). 
 
• Examples include molecules like H₂, O₂, N₂, and CH₄. 
 
• Depending on the number of shared electron pairs, covalent bonds can be classified as single, double, or triple bonds. 
 
 
 
• **Types of Covalent Bonds:** 
 
 
• **Single Bond:** Involves one shared pair of electrons (e.g., H₂, Cl₂). 
 
• **Double Bond:** Involves two shared pairs of electrons (e.g., O₂, CO₂). 
 
• **Triple Bond:** Involves three shared pairs of electrons (e.g., N₂, C₂H₂). 
 
 
 
• **Electron Pair Sharing:** 
 
 
• Each shared electron pair corresponds to a covalent bond. 
 
• In molecules with multiple bonds (double or triple), more electron pairs are shared compared to single bonds. 
 
 
 
• **Stability of Covalent Compounds:** 
 
 
• The stability of a covalent compound depends on the strength of its bonds. Triple bonds (e.g., in N₂) are stronger than double or single bonds. 
 
• Hydrogen (H₂), having a single bond, is less complex in terms of shared electron pairs. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 

 
 
• **H₂:** The simplest molecule, involving only one shared pair of electrons, making it the molecule with the least number of shared electron pairs in the given options. 
 
• **Bond Order:** The number of shared pairs of electrons correlates directly with the bond order (e.g., single bond = bond order 1, double bond = bond order 2). 
 
• **Applications:** Hydrogen (H₂) is widely used in industries (e.g., ammonia production, hydrogen fuel cells) due to its simple molecular structure and chemical properties.

questions.question: Which of the following structures is present at the surface of the rough endoplasmic reticulum membrane?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ribosome**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Ribosomes** are present on the surface of the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER), giving it its "rough" appearance.
 
• The rough endoplasmic reticulum is involved in the **synthesis of proteins** that are destined for secretion, membrane incorporation, or lysosomal use.
 
• **Ribosomes** bind to the membrane of the RER through specific receptors during the process of protein translation.
 
• Proteins synthesized by ribosomes on the RER are transported into the lumen of the RER for **post-translational modification**.
 
• The presence of ribosomes distinguishes the rough endoplasmic reticulum from the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, which is involved in lipid synthesis and lacks ribosomes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER):**
 
 
• The endoplasmic reticulum is a membranous network within eukaryotic cells that plays a critical role in **protein and lipid synthesis**.
 
• It is divided into two types: **rough ER** (with ribosomes) and **smooth ER** (without ribosomes).
 
• The ER also assists in the transportation of substances within the cell and provides a site for biochemical reactions.
 
 
 
• **Ribosomes:**
 
 
• **Ribosomes** are molecular machines responsible for **protein synthesis** by translating messenger RNA (mRNA).
 
• They are found either freely floating in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
 
• Ribosomes are composed of **ribosomal RNA (rRNA)** and proteins and exist as two subunits (small and large).
 
 
 
• **Protein Synthesis:**
 
 
• The process of protein synthesis involves **transcription** (DNA to mRNA) and **translation** (mRNA to protein).
 
• Ribosomes play a critical role in translation, where they assemble amino acids into polypeptide chains based on the mRNA sequence.
 
 
 
• **Other Cellular Structures:**

• **Sexual reproduction results in greater variation among offspring** because it involves the **combination of genetic material from two individuals.** This process ensures the mixing of genes, leading to unique genetic combinations in the offspring. 
 
• Each parent contributes **half of their genetic material** to the offspring through specialized reproductive cells called gametes (sperm and egg). This recombination during fertilization is the basis for genetic diversity. 
 
• **Meiosis**, a special type of cell division, plays a crucial role in sexual reproduction by producing gametes with a unique set of genetic material. This includes processes like crossing over and independent assortment of chromosomes, which further enhance variation. 
 
• Genetic variation is important for the **adaptation and survival** of species in changing environments. It allows populations to evolve and develop resistance to diseases, environmental changes, and other challenges.
 
• Unlike asexual reproduction, which produces genetically identical offspring, sexual reproduction introduces new traits and characteristics in each generation, enhancing the species' genetic diversity.

• Promotes genetic diversity within a population.

• Requires two parents, unlike asexual reproduction, which involves only one parent.

• Independent assortment of chromosomes during meiosis ensures that each gamete receives a unique combination of genetic material. 
 
• These processes create a wide range of genetic combinations, contributing to the diversity seen in sexually reproducing populations.

• Genetic diversity enhances a species' ability to survive environmental changes and adapt to new conditions.

• Asexual reproduction involves a single parent and produces offspring that are genetically identical to the parent. 
 
• While it is faster and requires less energy, it does not contribute to genetic diversity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 

• The problem is based on **Ohm's Law**, which states that the current (I) through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to the voltage (V) across the two points and inversely proportional to the resistance (R) of the conductor. 

• The mathematical representation of Ohm's Law is: **V = I × R**, where: 
 
 
• **V** is the voltage in volts (V). 
 
• **I** is the current in amperes (A). 
 
• **R** is the resistance in ohms (Ω). 
 
 

• In the given problem: 
 
 
• **Voltage (V) = 6 V**. 
 
• **Current (I) = 2 A**. 
 
 

• To calculate resistance (R): 
 
 
• Rearranging the formula: **R = V / I**. 
 
• Substituting the given values: **R = 6 / 2 = 3 Ω**. 
 
 

• Therefore, the resistance of the wire is **3 Ω**, which corresponds to **Option 3**__. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **Ohm's Law:** 
 
 
• It was formulated by **Georg Simon Ohm** in 1827. 
 
• The law is fundamental in electrical engineering and circuit theory. 
 
• It applies to linear resistive circuits where the relationship between voltage, current, and resistance is constant. 
 
• Non-linear components like diodes or transistors do not follow Ohm’s Law. 
 
 

• **Resistance:** 
 
 
• Resistance is the measure of the opposition to the flow of electric current in a conductor. 
 
• It is measured in **ohms (Ω)**, named after Georg Simon Ohm. 
 
• Factors affecting resistance: 
 
 
• **Material:** Conductors (e.g., copper) have low resistance, while insulators (e.g., rubber) have high resistance. 
 
• **Length:** Resistance increases with the length of the conductor. 
 
• **Cross-sectional area:** Resistance decreases with an increase in the area of the conductor. 
 
• **Temperature:** For most conductors, resistance increases with temperature. 
 
 
 
 

• **Applications of Ohm's Law:** 
 
 
• Used in designing electrical and electronic circuits. 
 
• Helps in calculating the required resistance, current, or voltage for circuit components. 
 
• Essential for determining power consumption using the formula: **P = V × I**. 
 
 

• **Real-life Example:** 
 
 
• Consider a household electric bulb. If the bulb operates at **220 V** and draws a current of **0.5 A**, its resistance can be calculated using Ohm's Law: 
 
 
• **R = V / I = 220 / 0.5 = 440 Ω**.

• **Power formula:** 
 
 
• Electrical power (P) is calculated as: **P = V × I** or **P = I² × R** or **P = V² / R**. 
 
 

• **Kirchhoff's Laws:** 
 
 
• **Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL):** The total current entering a junction equals the total current leaving the junction. 
 
• **Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL):** The sum of all voltages around a closed loop equals zero. 
 
• Ohm's Law is often used alongside Kirchhoff’s Laws in circuit analysis. 
 
 

• **Practical Limitations:** 
 
 
• Ohm's Law does not apply to non-linear and time-variant components like diodes, transistors, and thermistors. 
 
• For alternating current (AC) circuits, impedance (Z) replaces resistance (R), and the relationship becomes **V = I × Z**.

• **Continuous motion:** Particles of matter are always in random motion due to the presence of kinetic energy. Their speed increases with an increase in temperature. 
 
• **Interparticle spaces:** Particles of matter have spaces between them. The extent of these spaces varies in solids, liquids, and gases. 
 
• **Forces of attraction:** There are intermolecular forces of attraction between the particles, which are strongest in solids, moderate in liquids, and weakest in gases. 
 
 

 
• **Examples of particle motion:** 
 
 
• **Diffusion:** The movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration, such as the spreading of a drop of ink in water. 
 
• **Brownian motion:** The random movement of particles in a fluid (liquid or gas) due to collisions with other particles.

• **Solids:** Particles are tightly packed, with minimal motion (vibration in fixed positions). 
 
• **Liquids:** Particles can slide past each other, allowing liquids to flow.

• **Temperature effect:** The kinetic energy of particles increases with temperature, leading to faster movement and greater diffusion rates.

questions.question: Which of the following explains the absence of recessive traits in the F₁ generation and their reappearance in the F₂ generation in Mendal’s experiment?

options.text: Recessive traits are completely destroyed in the F₁ generation
Recessive traits become dominant in F₂ generation.
Recessive alleles are hidden in F₁ but reappear in F₂ due to segregation.

questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In Mendel’s experiments, **recessive traits** were not observed in the F₁ generation because **dominant alleles mask the expression of recessive alleles**.
 
• Mendel proposed the **Law of Segregation**, which states that allele pairs separate during gamete formation, ensuring that each gamete carries only one allele for each gene.
 
• In the F₁ generation, individuals are heterozygous (carry one dominant and one recessive allele), but the recessive trait remains hidden because the dominant allele determines the phenotype.
 
• When F₁ individuals are self-crossed, the alleles segregate independently, resulting in the **reappearance of the recessive trait** in the F₂ generation in a phenotypic ratio of **3:1 (dominant:recessive)**.
 
• This reappearance of recessive traits in F₂ demonstrates the **inheritance of alleles as discrete units**, as explained by Mendel’s principles.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Dominant and Recessive Alleles:**
 
 
• **Dominant alleles** are expressed in the phenotype even if only one copy is present (e.g., **T** for tall plants).
 
• **Recessive alleles** are only expressed when two copies are present (e.g., **t** for short plants).
 
• Mendel used symbols like **T** (dominant) and **t** (recessive) to represent alleles.
 
 
 
• **F₁ and F₂ Generations:**
 
 
• F₁ generation results from the crossing of two **pure-breeding (homozygous) parents** (e.g., **TT x tt**).
 
• F₂ generation results from self-pollination of F₁ plants, showing a **3:1 phenotypic ratio**.
 
 
 
• **Mendel’s Laws:**
 
 
• **Law of Segregation:** Each individual carries two alleles for a trait, which segregate during gamete formation.
 
• **Law of Independent Assortment:** Genes for different traits assort independently of one another during gamete formation (applies when genes are on different chromosomes).
 
 
 
• **Significance of Mendel’s Work:**
 
 
• Mendel’s experiments laid the foundation for the modern field of **genetics**.
 
• He demonstrated that inheritance follows specific, predictable patterns, which led to the development of **Punnett squares** and other genetic tools.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Mendel’s Pea Plant Experiment:**
 
 
• Mendel chose **pea plants (Pisum sativum)** for his experiments because they had easily observable traits like **flower color** and **seed shape**.
 
• He conducted **cross-pollination** and **self-pollination** experiments to study inheritance patterns.
 
• He studied **seven contrasting traits**, such as tall vs. short plants and yellow vs. green seeds.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Recessive Traits:**
 
 
• Recessive traits provide evidence that genetic information is passed down in **pairs of alleles**.
 
• Their reappearance in F₂ supports the concept of **genetic segregation and recombination**.
 
 
 
• **Modern Genetic Insights:**
 
 
• Mendel’s principles were later supported by the discovery of **DNA** and the molecular basis of genetics.

• The entire process is conducted in electrolytic cells, such as the mercury cell, diaphragm cell, or membrane cell, depending on the specific setup.

__
 
• **Electrolytic Cell Setup:**
 
 
• The electrolytic cell used in the chlor-alkali process has two electrodes: **anode** (positively charged) and **cathode** (negatively charged).
 
• Brine solution (NaCl) is used as the electrolyte, which dissociates into Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in water.
 
 
 
• **Products of the Chlor-Alkali Process:**
 
 
• **Chlorine gas (Cl₂):** Released at the anode and used in industries for making PVC, disinfectants, and bleaches.
 
• **Hydrogen gas (H₂):** Released at the cathode and used in fuel cells, ammonia production, and hydrogenation of fats and oils.
 
• **Sodium hydroxide (NaOH):** Remains in the solution and is used in paper manufacturing, soap making, and water treatment.
 
 
 
• **Electrochemical Reactions:**
 
 
• **At the anode (oxidation):** 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ (Chlorine gas is released).
 
• **At the cathode (reduction):** 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻ (Hydrogen gas and hydroxide ions are formed).
 
 
 
• **Applications of Chlorine Gas:**
 
 
• Used in the production of **polyvinyl chloride (PVC)**, which is used in pipes, cables, and packaging materials.
 
• Essential in the manufacture of **bleaches** like sodium hypochlorite and calcium hypochlorite.
 
• Used as a disinfectant in water treatment plants to kill bacteria and viruses.
 
 
 
• **Environmental Concerns:**
 
 
• The chlor-alkali process can lead to the release of harmful by-products if not properly managed, such as mercury and chlorine gas leaks.

• **Mercury Cell Process:**
 
 
• In this method, mercury acts as the cathode, and chlorine gas is released at the anode.
 
• However, it poses environmental risks due to mercury contamination.
 
 
 
• **Diaphragm Cell Process:**
 
 
• It uses a porous diaphragm to separate the anode and cathode compartments, preventing the mixing of chlorine and hydroxide ions.
 
• This ensures the purity of sodium hydroxide produced.
 
 
 
• **Membrane Cell Process:**
 
 
• A modern and environmentally friendly method that uses a selective ion-exchange membrane to separate the compartments.
 
• This process achieves high efficiency and eliminates the need for mercury or asbestos diaphragms.
 
 
 
• **Industrial Use of By-products:**
 
 
• **Hydrogen gas:** Used as a clean energy source in various industrial applications.
 
• **Sodium hydroxide:** Widely used in textiles, detergents, and paper manufacturing industries.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly explains the phenomenon of dispersion?

options.text: Dispersion is the bouncing back of light when it strikes a surface.
Dispersion is the scattering of light by colloidal particles.
Dispersion is the bending of light as a light ray of single wavelength goes from one medium to another.
Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its seven constituent colours as it passes through a glass prism.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its seven constituent colours as it passes through a glass prism.**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 

__ 
 
• **Dispersion** refers to the phenomenon where **white light splits into its seven constituent colours** (Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red) when it passes through a medium such as a prism. 
 
• This occurs because different colours of light have different **wavelengths**, and each wavelength bends by a different amount when passing through the prism, causing the light to spread out into a spectrum. 
 
• The **index of refraction** of a material (e.g., glass) depends on the wavelength of the light, leading to varying degrees of bending for each colour. For instance, **violet light bends the most**, while **red light bends the least**. 
 
• This principle is why we observe natural phenomena like **rainbows**, where sunlight is dispersed by water droplets in the atmosphere. 
 
• The splitting of white light into its constituent colours is an example of **refraction**, but it specifically highlights the wavelength dependence of the refractive index, which is the essence of dispersion. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 

__

• **Option 1:** Dispersion is not the **bouncing back of light** when it strikes a surface. This phenomenon is called **reflection**. Hence, this option is incorrect. 
 
• **Option 2:** Dispersion is not the **scattering of light by colloidal particles**. This is known as **scattering of light**, which explains phenomena like the blue colour of the sky. Hence, this option is incorrect. 
 
• **Option 3:** Dispersion is not simply the **bending of light** as a single wavelength passes from one medium to another. This is called **refraction**. Dispersion specifically involves the splitting of light into its spectrum. Hence, this option is also incorrect. 
 
• **Option 5:** This option is left blank in the question and does not provide any explanation or statement to consider. Hence, it is not applicable. 
 
 
 
• **Applications of Dispersion:** 
 
 
• **Rainbows:** Formed when sunlight undergoes dispersion through water droplets in the atmosphere. 
 
• **Spectroscopy:** Used in scientific instruments to analyze light spectra, helping in the identification of materials. 
 
• **Prism Experiments:** Commonly used in physics to demonstrate the splitting of light into its constituent colours. 
 
 
 
• **Important Properties Related to Dispersion:** 
 
 
• **Refractive Index Dependence:** The refractive index varies for different wavelengths of light, which is the primary cause of dispersion. 
 
• **Angular Separation:** The angular separation of colours depends on the material of the prism and the angle of incidence of light. 
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:** 
 
 
• **Isaac Newton:** First demonstrated dispersion using a glass prism in the 17th century, showing that white light is composed of different colours. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 

 
 
• **Order of Colours in Dispersion:** The colours always appear in the order: **Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red** (VIBGYOR). 
 
• **Angle of Deviation:** Violet light experiences the **greatest angle of deviation** because it has the shortest wavelength, while red light has the **smallest deviation**. 
 
• **Natural Examples:** Dispersion is responsible for phenomena like **fireworks**, where different chemicals produce different colours due to the dispersion of light. 
 
• **Relation to Wavelength:** Shorter wavelengths (e.g., violet) are refracted more than longer wavelengths (e.g., red), highlighting the dependence of dispersion on wavelength.

questions.question: What is the primary role of a 'functional group' in an organic compound?

options.text: To change the carbon chain from straight to branched
To determine the physical state (solid, liquid, gas) of the compound
To provide the characteristic chemical properties of the compound
To increase the molecular mass of the compound

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To provide the characteristic chemical properties of the compound**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Functional groups** are specific groups of atoms within molecules that are responsible for the characteristic chemical reactions of those molecules.
 
• The presence of a functional group determines the **chemical properties and reactivity** of the compound, such as its ability to undergo specific chemical reactions.
 
• Common examples of functional groups include hydroxyl (-OH), carbonyl (C=O), carboxyl (-COOH), amine (-NH2), and alkene (-C=C-).
 
• Functional groups influence the behavior of organic compounds in chemical reactions, such as **nucleophilic substitution, elimination, or addition reactions.**
 
• For instance, the hydroxyl group (-OH) in alcohols makes them polar and capable of forming hydrogen bonds, which directly affects their solubility and boiling points.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Key Features of Functional Groups:**
 
 
• Functional groups determine the **chemical reactivity and physical properties** of a molecule.
 
• They often participate in specific types of chemical reactions, such as **acid-base reactions, oxidation-reduction, and polymerization.**
 
• Examples of functional group reactions include the esterification of carboxylic acids and the hydration of alkenes.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Functional Groups:**
 
 
• **Alcohol (-OH):** Found in ethanol, responsible for its polar nature and hydrogen bonding.
 
• **Carbonyl (C=O):** Found in aldehydes and ketones, influencing their reactivity in nucleophilic addition reactions.
 
• **Carboxyl (-COOH):** Present in carboxylic acids, contributing to their acidic properties.
 
• **Amine (-NH2):** Found in amino acids, playing a role in their basicity and nucleophilicity.
 
 
 
• **Role in Organic Chemistry:**
 
 
• Functional groups are used to classify and name organic compounds under the IUPAC nomenclature system.
 
• They are essential in determining the reactivity patterns of molecules in **synthetic organic chemistry.**
 
• Understanding functional groups is crucial in fields such as **pharmaceutical chemistry, biochemistry, and material science.**
 
 
 
• **Applications of Functional Groups:**
 
 
• Functional groups are used in designing drugs, as their interactions with biological targets depend on specific groups.
 
• They play a vital role in polymer chemistry, such as the formation of polyethylene or nylon.
 
• Functional groups are critical in determining the **spectroscopic properties** of molecules, aiding in their identification through IR, NMR, and UV-Vis spectroscopy.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Option 1:** Changing the carbon chain from straight to branched affects the molecule's structure but is not the primary role of functional groups. *Hence, this option is incorrect.*
 
• **Option 2:** Physical state (solid, liquid, gas) is influenced by intermolecular forces like hydrogen bonding or van der Waals forces, not directly by functional groups. *Hence, this option is incorrect.*
 
• **Option 4:** Increasing molecular mass depends on the number of atoms, not solely on functional groups. *Hence, this option is incorrect.*
 
• **Option 5:** This option does not exist in the question and is irrelevant. *Hence, it is not applicable.*

__ 

• **Plastic bags** are made from synthetic polymers derived from petroleum, such as polyethylene, which are non-biodegradable in nature. 

• They do not decompose easily and can persist in the environment for hundreds of years, contributing significantly to pollution. 

• Unlike organic materials such as **silk, jute, or cotton**, plastic bags are resistant to biological degradation, making them a major environmental hazard. 

• Plastic bags often break down into microplastics under sunlight, which further contaminates soil and water systems. 

• The durability and resistance of plastic bags to natural decomposition make them unsuitable for sustainable environmental practices. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **Silk Cloth Bag:** 
 

• Silk is a natural protein fiber obtained from silkworms and is biodegradable. 

• Silk cloth bags decompose easily in the environment within a few months under favorable conditions. 

• They are a sustainable alternative to plastic bags and are widely used for premium packaging. 
 
 

• **Jute Bag:** 
 

• Jute is a natural fiber grown in countries like **India** and **Bangladesh**, known for its biodegradable properties. 

• Jute bags decompose within a few weeks to months and do not harm the environment. 

• Due to its eco-friendly nature, jute is often promoted as a sustainable option for daily use. 
 
 

• **Cotton Cloth Bag:** 
 

• Cotton is a natural fiber derived from the cotton plant and is biodegradable. 

• Cotton cloth bags take a few months to decompose and are considered environmentally friendly. 

• They are reusable and widely used as alternatives to plastic bags for grocery shopping and storage. 
 
 

• **Environmental Impact of Plastic Bags:** 
 

• Plastic bags contribute to **soil, water, and air pollution** and are one of the major causes of clogged drainage systems. 

• They pose threats to wildlife as animals often ingest plastic, mistaking it for food, leading to fatal consequences. 

• Globally, efforts are being made to ban or limit the use of plastic bags to promote sustainable alternatives. 

• Examples include bans on single-use plastics in countries like **India (2019)** and the European Union's initiatives to reduce plastic waste.

• **Biodegradable vs. Non-Biodegradable:** 
 

• **Biodegradable materials** like jute, cotton, and silk break down naturally through microbial activity, causing minimal environmental harm. 

• **Non-biodegradable materials** like plastic persist for decades to centuries, leading to long-term environmental damage. 
 
 

• **Government Initiatives:** 
 

• Many governments globally have introduced bans on plastic bags to combat pollution. For example, India imposed a ban on single-use plastic items from **July 1, 2022**. 

• Awareness campaigns and subsidies are being provided to promote eco-friendly alternatives like jute and cloth bags. 
 
 

• **Global Plastic Waste Statistics:** 
 

• According to the **United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP)**, around **300 million tons** of plastic waste is generated every year globally. 

• Less than **10%** of plastic waste is recycled, with the majority ending up in landfills or oceans.

questions.question: External fertilisation is found in which of the following organisms?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Fish**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 

• **External fertilization** is a reproductive process where the fertilization of the egg occurs outside the body of the organism. It typically happens in an aquatic environment. 

• Among the options provided, **Fish** exhibit external fertilization. Female fish release eggs into the water, and male fish release sperm over the eggs to fertilize them externally. This process ensures a higher chance of fertilization in aquatic conditions. 

• Other organisms listed, such as **Humans**, **Hens**, and **Cows**, exhibit **internal fertilization**, where the fusion of sperm and egg occurs inside the body of the female. 

• External fertilization is common in aquatic organisms like fish, amphibians, and some invertebrates because water facilitates the movement of gametes and prevents them from drying out. 

• The process of external fertilization has both advantages, such as producing a large number of offspring, and disadvantages, including the vulnerability of gametes and embryos to environmental hazards and predators. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **External Fertilization:** 
 

• External fertilization occurs in water or moist environments to protect gametes from desiccation and to allow sperm to swim to eggs. 

• The process is less energy-intensive for the parents compared to internal fertilization, but it often results in lower survival rates due to environmental threats. 

• Examples of organisms exhibiting external fertilization include **fish** (like salmon and cod), **amphibians** (like frogs), and certain invertebrates (like sea urchins). 

• The fertilized eggs or embryos are often left to develop independently, with limited or no parental care. 
 
 

• **Internal Fertilization:** 
 

• In internal fertilization, fertilization occurs inside the female’s body. This method is more common in terrestrial animals to prevent gametes from drying out. 

• Organisms such as **Humans**, **Cows**, and **Hens** exhibit internal fertilization. 

• Internal fertilization provides better protection to the developing embryo and often involves significant parental investment. 

• Examples of internal fertilization include mammals (like humans and cows), birds (like hens), and reptiles. 
 
 

• **Comparison:** 
 

• **External fertilization** often produces a large number of offspring, but survival rates can be low due to environmental threats and lack of parental care. 

• **Internal fertilization** produces fewer offspring, but survival rates are higher due to better protection and care provided to the embryos. 
 
 

• **Fish Reproduction:** 
 

• Most fish exhibit external fertilization, though some species (like guppies and sharks) perform internal fertilization. 

• Fish that use external fertilization typically release eggs and sperm simultaneously into the water during spawning. 

• Environmental factors such as temperature, salinity, and water currents can significantly affect the success of external fertilization in fish. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 

• **Examples of External Fertilization in Fish:** 
 

• Species like **salmon**, **cod**, and **carp** are known for external fertilization. 

• These species often migrate to specific spawning grounds to maximize the chances of successful fertilization. 
 
 

• **Adaptations for External Fertilization:** 
 

• Many aquatic species produce a large number of gametes to increase the likelihood of successful fertilization. 

• The timing of gamete release is often synchronized to ensure that eggs and sperm meet. 
 
 

• **Disadvantages of External Fertilization:** 
 

• Gametes and embryos are exposed to predators and environmental hazards. 

• There is limited parental care, which reduces the survival rate of offspring.
